title: How Does a ZIP File Make Files Smaller?
sources: Wikipedia, 'Deflate' (the default ZIP method): lossless; combines LZ77 and Huffman coding; LZ77 replaces repeated strings with back-references (length, distance) to an earlier copy; Huffman gives frequent symbols shorter bit codes; designed by Phil Katz for PKZIP 2
zlib.net, Antaeus Feldspar, 'An Explanation of the Deflate Algorithm': repeated strings replaced by pointers back to an earlier occurrence; common symbols get shorter codes

Wikipedia, 'Zip bomb': 42.zip is 42 kilobytes of compressed data, five layers of nested zip files in sets of 16, each bottom layer a 4.3 GB file, 4.5 petabytes in total when fully unpacked (4.5 PB = about 4.5 million GB)
Wikipedia, 'Lossless compression': files with repeated data compress well; already-compressed data (JPEG photos, MP4 video) barely shrinks

lines.text: How does a zip file make your files smaller without losing a single bit?
lines.caps: HOW DOES A *ZIP | MAKE YOUR *FILES | *SMALLER | WITHOUT *LOSING | A SINGLE *BIT?

lines.text: Well, most files are full of repeats,
the same words and patterns again and again.
So zip writes each pattern just once,
and every repeat becomes a tiny note:
Then the most common letters get the shortest codes,
like nicknames for your best friends.
Unzip it, and your computer follows the notes
The twist? A famous file called forty-two dot zip
but fully unzipped, it would fill millions of gigabytes.
So a zip isn't magic, it's just really good note taking.
lines.caps: SO A *ZIP | ISN'T *MAGIC | IT'S *JUST | REALLY *GOOD | *NOTE TAKING
